_comment: Which consumer each public capability must reach, so that "implemented" and "shipped" stop being the same word.
每个 public 能力必须到达哪一类消费者——这样「实现了」和「出货了」才不是同一句话。
Four classes, because they fail differently:
* `motor-owned` -- the library's own loop must contain it, so it has to be reachable from a production
translation unit under `src/`. Unreachable is a defect: the header exists, the tests are green, and a
user of the released package cannot get at it (`stall_start.hpp` was exactly this);
* `diagnostic` -- only useful if something can read it out, so each `abi` name must exist in the C surface;
* `contract` -- a port is a promise, and `stub` names the reference implementation that proves the promise
* `policy` -- composed by the host, so reachability from `src/` is *not* expected; what it owes instead is a
runnable example. `example: null` is allowed and counted, because "no example yet" and "we did not think
about it" must not look the same in a file;
* `todo` -- not decided yet. Counted every run against `todo_baseline`, which may only fall.
`known_unshipped` is the honest debt list: a `motor-owned` header that nothing in `src/` reaches, with the batch
that fixes it. It is a ratchet in both directions -- an entry whose header has become reachable is itself a
failure, because a stale exception hides the next real one.
This gate is the STATIC half of the rule. The dynamic half ("switch the thing off and the output must move")
is a test convention, not a gate: `blast` and `wired` both answer "is the wire there", neither answers "is the
thing on the other end right".

core/deadtime.hpp.why: the loss model is applied by the caller before modulating: `Svpwm` sees no phase currents, so this release has no production slot for it

core/friction_comp.hpp.why: a feed-forward the caller adds to its torque command; `Motor` has no compensation slot, which is why nothing in `src/` includes it

core/bus_current_limit.hpp.why: the caller scales its own command with it; whether a bus current can be measured at all, and what ceiling the supply allows, are facts about the installation, so this type takes both as inputs and nothing in `src/` includes it

core/angle_source.hpp.why: the caller feeds it the offers it actually has and applies the answer; which sources a drive has, and in what order it trusts them, is a fact about the drive, so this type takes the order as an argument rather than assuming one -- which is also why nothing in `src/` includes it

core/gear_ratio.hpp.why: a coordinate transform between the caller's units and the axis; by design it lives on the caller's side of the boundary

core/hall.hpp.why: there is no HAL input for the three pins yet (batch 1 adds one), so a host has to write its own reader even though the decoder ships

core/soft_limit.hpp.why: a limiter the caller applies to its own position commands; `Motor` takes commands already limited

core/trace.hpp.why: the recorder is only useful if something can read it out, so its reachability is the C ABI shape of it

motor/drive_supervisor.hpp.why: the caller wraps its own `Motor` in it, which is why nothing in `src/` includes it and why `motor.hpp` was not touched: the tick order is a decision about the *application's* hardware (which fault pin, which chopper, which temperature channel), and a `Motor` that assumed one would have taken that decision away from every host that does it differently

hal/mechanical_brake.hpp.why: the device that holds a vertical load while the drive is off; the shipped stub is what proves the shape is implementable, including the two refusals a sequencer has to survive

hal/clock.hpp.why: a port is only a contract until something implements it; the stub is what proves the shape is implementable

hal/current_sense.hpp.why: a port is only a contract until something implements it; the stub is what proves the shape is implementable

hal/dc_link.hpp.why: a port is only a contract until something implements it; the stub is what proves the shape is implementable

hal/position.hpp.why: a port is only a contract until something implements it; the stub is what proves the shape is implementable

hal/pwm.hpp.why: a port is only a contract until something implements it; the stub is what proves the shape is implementable

api/foc_api.h.why: the C surface is the product path: a capability that is not reachable here is not shipped at all

version.h.why: the one string C and C++ share, on the same path

driver/callback_hal.hpp.why: a reference implementation of a contract: it is the example, so it owes being exercised rather than being documented

driver/scripted_current.hpp.why: a reference implementation of a contract: it is the example, so it owes being exercised rather than being documented

driver/sim_position.hpp.why: a reference implementation of a contract: it is the example, so it owes being exercised rather than being documented

driver/stub_dc_link.hpp.why: a reference implementation of a contract: it is the example, so it owes being exercised rather than being documented

driver/stub_hal.hpp.why: a reference implementation of a contract: it is the example, so it owes being exercised rather than being documented

driver/stub_pwm.hpp.why: a reference implementation of a contract: it is the example, so it owes being exercised rather than being documented

hal/hall.hpp.why: three bits is the whole interface a hall set offers; the decoder and the sequencing rule are ours, reading the pins is the host's

driver/stub_hall.hpp.why: a settable code so the policy can be exercised without a board, and it deliberately does not validate -- an illegal code reaching the policy is the policy's case

core/trace_parse.hpp.why: a host-side reader of the trace channel: the firmware never parses its own ring

comm/frame.hpp.why: a link layer the host drives; the firmware's control path never frames anything

comm/commissioned_set.hpp.why: a storage format: this module decides what the bytes are and refuses the ones no reader may accept, while where they live (flash, EEPROM, a file on a host) belongs to the integrator -- nothing on the control path encodes a record

core/thermistor.hpp.why: a datasheet-to-temperature conversion the integrator configures: the three numbers and which leg of the divider the part sits in are board facts, so nothing in the control path constructs one

hal/temperature.hpp.why: a winding-temperature channel is optional, and the contract exists so a consumer can ask whether one is present instead of assuming a number; a drive with no thermistor is legal

driver/stub_temperature.hpp.why: the reference implementation of the contract, starting invalid so a consumer that forgets to ask reads 'no measurement' rather than a temperature nobody set

comm/register_map.hpp.why: the protocol's view of the C surface: a host asks, the firmware answers, nothing in the loop calls it

core/min_pulse.hpp.why: the loss is what a caller must know *before* it commands: `Motor` has no slot for a driver limit, and only the plant can say what the driver actually did

core/brake_chopper.hpp.why: composed by the host into its own fault/supervisor path; the loop itself does not drive a chopper

core/single_shunt.hpp.why: a host whose current sense is one DC-link shunt composes it between the modulator and the loop; `Motor` has no slot for a reconstruction scheme, and the topology's blind spot is the host's problem to solve

core/mtpv.hpp.why: a host that wants to run above the base speed composes it where it builds its current reference: it needs the voltage ceiling and the current ceiling, neither of which `Motor` owns, and it reports which of the two decided the point so the host can tell "the voltage is what limits me" from "the current is"

core/cogging_comp.hpp.why: a host that wants the ripple gone composes it next to its current reference, where the mechanical angle and the d-axis current are both known; it returns an offset and reports its own fade and clipping, because a compensator that hides either looks like one that works

core/cogging_learn.hpp.why: a host that has no cogging data for its machine runs one learning pass with the compensator off and hands the table it gets back to `CoggingCompensation::set_table()` unchanged; it is a policy because the pass is a *run* the host schedules (spin, accumulate, finish), not something `Motor` should do inside a tick, and because its refusals are the host's to act on -- spin longer, slower, or steadier are three different actions

core/thermal_limit.hpp.why: a host that has to promise a duty asks it what current can be held forever and how long any other current may be held; it is a policy rather than a `Motor` concern because the answer depends on how the machine is mounted and cooled -- numbers the caller has and the drive does not -- and because the host is what decides what to do when the budget is short

core/auto_tune.hpp.why: a commissioning tool composes it, runs one torque-step window and applies the `Pi` config it gets back -- or applies it and gets nothing new when the pass refuses, because the gains it hands back are the nameplate ones. It is a policy because the pass is a *run* the host schedules and its refusals (spin with a varying current, stop if it saturates) are the host's to act on

comm/encoder_stream.hpp.why: a host that clocks an SSI/BiSS-style absolute encoder writes its own shift-register driver (the pin timing is the HAL's) and hands the collected bits here for interpretation; it is a policy because the framing -- start/ACK, stop, clock rate -- is the host's and this module must not pretend to own it, and because the multi-turn assembler needs the axis's maximum travel per frame, which only the application knows

core/watchdog.hpp.why: a host that has to stop a drive when its own feeder stalls asks it whether the silence is past the deadline and which cause it was; it is a policy rather than a `Motor` concern because the timestamp belongs to the host -- the library never reads a clock it does not own -- and because the host is what decides when to poll and which line raises the fault, so the module answers the cause and does not reach into the drive

core/move_trajectory.hpp.why: the caller streams its position into its own position loop and re-aims it when the target moves; what the axis can follow is a fact about the installation, so this type takes the limits as an input and nothing in `src/` includes it
